content.title: Does the resurrection really matter?
content.summary: Christ rose bodily. Our forgiveness and hope depend on it.

answer.text: Yes. Jesus actually rose from the dead, bodily and gloriously; Southern Baptists confess that he was raised “with a glorified body” (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article II). Paul says that without his resurrection faith would be futile and we would remain in our sins. The resurrection is God's saving act in history, not a metaphor for the disciples keeping Jesus' ideals alive.

reasoning.text: Paul passes on the message of Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection and appearances.
Luke presents Jesus showing his body and eating with his disciples.
Christ's resurrection is the beginning and guarantee of the resurrection of all who belong to him.

conclusion.text: The Christian hope rests in the risen Christ himself, not merely in the psychological value of believing a resurrection story.

sections.text: First Corinthians 15 reports appearances to named people and to a large group. It is Paul's account of witnesses; we do not possess 500 separate statements in that passage. A strong case should describe the evidence we actually have.
sections.title: Use the testimony accurately

sections.text: Read the accounts, examine objections and explain why the testimony is credible. Do not turn an argument into a substitute for God's authority or the Spirit's work. Christianity's supernatural claims cannot be removed while leaving its gospel intact.
sections.title: Historical reasoning serves the Word

sections.text: This article asks why the resurrection matters; whether it happened is argued in full in “Did Jesus rise? The historical case”. But the ground is worth knowing. Historians of very different convictions, believing and sceptical, broadly accept that Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate; that soon afterwards his followers were convinced they had seen him alive; that Paul, a persecutor, and James, Jesus' brother, came to the same conviction; and that the claim was made in Jerusalem within weeks. Many, though not all, add that the tomb was found empty. Paul himself passes on a summary he had received, naming Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James and all the apostles, and he had met Cephas and James in Jerusalem within a few years of the events. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, granted that Peter and Paul had experiences they took to be appearances of the risen Jesus, and explained them as visions. The disagreement is not over these facts but over their best explanation.
sections.title: What scholars across the spectrum accept

sections.text: Since the first Easter, those who did not believe have offered other explanations: the disciples stole the body, which Matthew records as the first one told; Jesus did not really die on the cross; the women went to the wrong tomb; the disciples had visions or hallucinations; or the story grew as a legend over decades. Each is set out with its holders and the reply in “Other explanations of Easter”. The common difficulty is that each explains one piece of the evidence and leaves the rest: a stolen body does not produce appearances, visions do not empty a tomb, and a slow legend does not fit a list of witnesses circulating within a few years.
sections.title: The main alternative explanations

sections.text: The New Testament does not describe a ghost or a resuscitated corpse. The risen Jesus is touched, eats, and bears the marks of the nails; yet he is no longer bound as before, and he does not die again. Paul calls the resurrection body imperishable, glorious and powerful, a “spiritual body”: not a body made of spirit, but a body wholly given life by the Spirit of God. The Baptist Faith and Message says Christ was raised “with a glorified body”. In first-century Jewish usage, as N. T. Wright has argued at length, “resurrection” meant a new bodily life after death, never a mere survival of the soul; that is why the apostles' claim was heard as a claim about the tomb.
sections.title: What kind of body?

sections.text: If Christ rose, then his death was not defeat: he was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification. God has given proof that he will judge the world by the man he has appointed. Those who belong to Christ will be raised as he was, since the same Spirit who raised him will give life to their mortal bodies. And death, the last enemy, has already been beaten in one man. Paul states the other side as bluntly: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and we are still in our sins. Christianity has staked itself on an event that could be checked.
sections.title: What follows if he rose

content.objection: Could the disciples simply have meant that Jesus' influence survived?

reply.text: That does not fit the claim of the texts: the tomb is empty, Jesus appears, and Paul ties his resurrection to our future bodily resurrection.

heldBy: Bart D. Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014)
objections.objection: Paul lists his own experience on the Damascus road alongside the others, and his was a vision of light and a voice. So the earliest “appearances” were visions, which grieving people commonly have; belief in a bodily resurrection and the empty-tomb stories grew up afterwards to express what the visions meant.

reply.text: Paul puts his experience last and calls it out of the ordinary, “as to one of untimely birth”. Grief visions come to individuals, usually to those who already loved the dead person; the list includes groups, a hostile persecutor and a sceptical brother. And visions of a dead man, however vivid, would have been called visions or an angel, not resurrection, a word that in Jewish use meant a body raised from the grave; the disciples first think they are seeing a spirit and are corrected. The empty tomb is in Mark and probably in the formula Paul received, which mentions burial before rising.

heldBy: Bart D. Ehrman (debate with W. L. Craig, 2006)
objections.objection: The four Easter accounts disagree on who went to the tomb, how many angels there were, and where Jesus first appeared, in Galilee or Jerusalem. Reimarus set them out one by one, and Bruno Bauer said in the 1840s that no one had refuted him. Witnesses who cannot agree on the basic story cannot be trusted on the miracle at its centre.

reply.text: The accounts do differ in detail, as independent reports of a confusing morning do; the earliest Gospel even ends with the women too afraid to speak. But they agree on the core: Jesus was buried, women found the tomb empty on the first day of the week, and he appeared to his followers. Historians do not discard an event because the reports of it vary in the details; they look for what the sources share. Simon Greenleaf, a Harvard professor of the law of evidence, argued in 1846, after Paley, that honest testimony shows “substantial truth under circumstantial variety”, and that strict verbal agreement between the accounts would make them less credible, not more.

heldBy: James George Frazer and the history-of-religions school (around 1900)
Richard Carrier (On the Historicity of Jesus, 2014)
objections.objection: The Mediterranean world was full of gods who died and rose again with the seasons: Osiris, Adonis, Attis, Tammuz. The Christian story is one more of these, dressed in Jewish clothing.

reply.text: The parallels are thinner than they sound. The nature deities did not die and rise as a historical person under a named Roman governor, and some of the “resurrections” appear only in sources later than the Gospels or in modern reconstructions. Scholars across the spectrum, including Ehrman, who is no believer, now reject the idea that the Easter proclamation was borrowed from them. The earliest Christians were Jews who thought of resurrection in Daniel's terms, the dead raised bodily at the end of the age, and who claimed that this had happened to one man ahead of time.

limit.text: A summary cannot settle every historical objection. Distinguish Scripture's testimony, your explanation of it and additional reconstructions that may remain uncertain.

prompt.text: Could we read the resurrection testimony and ask what difference it makes if Christ really rose?
